# The Hour That Belongs to No One

There is an hour that belongs to no one. It sits somewhere between one and four in the morning, depending on the city, the season, and the particular insomnia of the person walking through it. I have come to think of it as the most honest hour of the day, because nothing is performing for anything else. The restaurants have given up. The commuters are asleep or failing to be. Even the insomniacs have usually retreated behind curtains by then, leaving the streets to a sparse population of cab drivers, bakers, nurses walking home from shifts, and the occasional person like me, who has no good reason to be out and has stopped pretending otherwise.

I started walking at night years ago, not as exercise and not as a habit I could defend, but because I could not sleep and because lying in bed had become its own kind of work. There is only so long you can stare at a ceiling before the ceiling starts to feel like an accusation. So I would get up, put on whatever was nearest, and go out. The first thing you notice, if you do this enough, is that the city at that hour is not the same city. It is a rough draft of itself, the version before the editors arrive. The light is wrong in a way that makes familiar buildings look like photographs of themselves. The air has a temperature the daytime never admits to. And the silence is not silence at all. It is the sound of all the things the city does when it thinks no one is listening: the hum of transformers, the drip of a broken gutter, a train two neighborhoods away, your own footsteps, which suddenly have a volume and a character you had never been told about.

I want to write about what happens to a person out there, in that hour, because I think it is a stranger and more important experience than we usually give it credit for. And I want to write about it in a way that does not rush to turn it into a lesson. Some experiences are not lessons. They are just experiences, and they change you in ways you only notice later, the way you only notice a current by looking back at the shore.

The first thing that happens is that you become aware of your own attention. During the day, attention is a practical instrument. You point it at traffic, at emails, at the face of the person talking to you, and it does its job and asks no questions. But at three in the morning, on an empty street, attention has nothing assigned to it. So it begins to wander, and in wandering it starts to notice things that were always there. The way a streetlight makes a cone of visibility and then surrenders everything outside it to darkness. The way a cat on a fence evaluates you with the bored cruelty of a creature that has never once worried about its purpose in life. The way your own breathing sounds when it is the loudest thing for two blocks. This sounds small. It is not small. What you are noticing, without having a word for it yet, is that the world is always more than you are looking at. The daytime world is a summary. The night world is the full text, and most of it is irrelevant, and that is precisely what makes it feel true.

The second thing that happens is that you start to think thoughts you would not allow yourself during the day. I do not mean dark thoughts, or not only dark ones. I mean unfinished thoughts. During the day, a thought has to be useful. It has to lead somewhere, produce an email, justify itself. At night, a thought can just sit there, half-formed, and you can sit with it, and neither of you has to explain what you are doing. I have done some of my most important thinking on these walks, and almost none of it has been the kind of thinking that produces conclusions. It has been the kind of thinking that produces recognition. You remember a conversation from eleven years ago and finally understand what the other person was afraid of. You realize that a decision you have been calling practical was actually just fear wearing a practical outfit. You miss someone you have not thought about in years, and the missing is not a problem to be solved but a fact to be stood inside, the way you would stand inside a doorway during rain.

The third thing that happens, and this is the one I care about most, is that you begin to feel the other people who are not there. This is hard to explain. The empty street is not empty. It is full of absences that have shapes. There is the bakery on the corner, and you can feel the baker who is not yet there but will arrive in an hour, and you can feel the hundreds of mornings that have already happened in that room, the flour in the air, the specific complaints of the oven. There is the bus stop, and every person who has ever waited there is in some sense still waiting, layered into the glass and the dented sign. The city at night is a palimpsest. During the day the latest layer is all you see. At night the earlier layers show through, and you understand that you are walking through an enormous archive of other lives, none of which you will ever know, all of which were as real and urgent and particular as your own.

I had a moment on one of these walks that I have never been able to shake. I was crossing a street I had crossed ten thousand times, and I looked up at a lit window on the fourth floor of an ordinary building. Someone was awake. I could see only the shadow of a lamp and the edge of a curtain, no person, but I knew someone was there because the light had the quality of light that is being used rather than light that is merely on. And I was suddenly flooded with an awareness so complete it was almost physical: that behind that window was a whole life. A whole interior. A history of hurts and jokes and private nicknames and unresolved arguments and a body that had been carrying that person around since the day they were born. A whole world, in the technical sense, a center of experience from which my entire universe was just a street they sometimes walked down. And then I looked down the block and realized every dark window was the same. And every building. And every street in the city, and every city. The sheer quantity of inner life happening at that moment, almost all of it unknown, almost all of it unfinished, almost all of it never to be recorded anywhere, was more than I could hold. I stood in the crosswalk longer than I should have. Then the light changed, though there were no cars, and I crossed, and I have been trying to write my way back to that moment ever since.

We use the word "everyone" constantly. Everyone knows that. Everyone feels that way sometimes. Everyone is just trying to get through the day. But almost no one has any real sense of what everyone means. Everyone is an abstraction that we use to keep from being crushed by the actual arithmetic. The actual arithmetic is that there are billions of first-person perspectives currently operating, each one as vivid from the inside as yours is from the inside, each one containing a complete childhood, a set of beliefs that feel like perceptions, a private vocabulary of things they cannot easily say, a relationship to their own body that no one else will ever fully share, and a way of experiencing a rainy Tuesday or a song on the radio that is theirs alone. And most of those perspectives will live and die without ever being understood by more than a handful of other perspectives, and some by none.

I think about this a great deal now, not just at night. It has made me stranger to other people, I suspect, and also more patient. When someone cuts me off in traffic or is cruel in a comment section or is merely boring at a dinner party, I try to remember that I am looking at a entire universe of experience that I will never have access to, a universe that has reasons, and those reasons may be stupid or petty or broken, but they are reasons, they are the output of a whole life of causes. This does not always make me kinder. I am not writing this to claim that it does. But it makes me slower to conclude that I have understood someone, and that slowness feels like one of the few honest things about me.

There is a related thing I have noticed about how we treat our own inner lives. We are embarrassed by them. We have a private sense of how strange it is to be us, how discontinuous, how full of leftover feelings and unmotivated sadnesses and sudden joys that would be mortifying to explain. We assume everyone else is more coherent. We believe, in a low-level, unexamined way, that other people experience themselves as a clean narrative, a person with a career and a personality and a set of opinions, while we alone are a weather system. But this is a fiction produced by the fact that we only ever see other people from the outside, in edited form, in the version they can manage in public. The night walk dissolves this a little, because at night you remember that all those lit and unlit windows contain weather systems too. The clean narrative is a costume that everyone wears in the daytime and takes off in the hour that belongs to no one.

I am not sure where I am going with this, and that feels appropriate. The hour itself does not go anywhere. It is not a journey. It is a condition. You walk, you notice, you feel the weight of other lives and the strangeness of your own, and then the sky does its slow gray thing at the edge of the east, and the bakers arrive, and the first bus sighs at the corner, and the city begins its performance again, and you go home and sleep, finally, like a child after a secret.

But I want to say one more thing, about solitude, because people assume the night walk is lonely and I want to be precise. Loneliness is the pain of wanting connection and not having it. Solitude is something else. Solitude is the experience of being with yourself when no one is watching, and it is one of the few remaining experiences that has not been fully optimized, monetized, or narrated. In that hour, you are not a profile, not a role, not a node. You are a body moving through cold air, thinking thoughts that no one will audit. That is rare now. It may have been rare always. I think people used to get more of it, in the days before the feed, before the gentle insistence that every moment be either shared or felt guilty about not sharing. The night does not ask you to share. The night has no comment field. You can have a revelation on a dark street and tell no one, and the revelation is no less real for that. It might be more real. Some things shrink when they are explained, and grow when they are kept.

I still walk at night, less often than I used to, because I sleep better now, which is a gain I suppose, though I am not entirely sure it is. There is something the insomnia gave me that I did not know I was receiving. The walks were the tuition I paid, unknowingly, for a kind of education. I learned that the world is mostly invisible to me. I learned that other people are mostly invisible to each other. I learned that my own mind, left unwatched, will show me things that the watched mind will not. I learned that a city is a confession of everyone who ever needed to get somewhere. I learned that being alive is an extremely strange arrangement that we have all agreed not to discuss in any depth, probably because discussing it in depth would make ordinary life impossible, and ordinary life has things that need doing.

The hour that belongs to no one still comes, every night, whether I am out in it or not. It comes over every city and every town and every stretch of highway and every quiet farm. It comes over hospitals and prisons and hotels and homes where someone is sitting up with a child, and homes where someone is sitting up with a fear they have not named. It is the most democratic hour. It finds everyone eventually. And in it, the great performance pauses, and what is left is just the fact of millions of people, unconscious or nearly, holding their small fires of consciousness through the dark, each one a whole world, each one sure, in the way we are all sure without evidence, that they are the one who is real.

I do not have a conclusion. I have the memory of cold air and a lit window and the feeling of being a single attention in a dark that was full of other attentions, all of us unknown to each other, all of us real. If there is anything I would pass along, it is only this: that the full text of the world is always there, under the summary, and that occasionally, in the hour that belongs to no one, you are allowed to see it. And that seeing it changes the daylight, a little, if you let it. Not enough. But a little. And a little is not nothing.
